In [[topology]], a '''continuous group action''' is a [[Group action (mathematics)|group action]] adapted to the topological setting: <math>G</math> is a [[topological group]], <math>X</math> is a [[topological space]], and the action map is [[Continuous function|continuous]].

== Definition ==
Let
:<math>\Phi: G \times X \to X, \quad (g, x) \mapsto g \cdot x</math>
be a (left) group action of a topological group on a topological space; it is called a '''continuous group action''' if the map <math>\Phi</math> is continuous (with respect to the product topology on <math>G \times X</math>). A topological space endowed with a continuous group action is also called a ''<math>G</math>'''''-space'''.

=== Properties ===
A continuous action is automatically an '''action by homeomorphisms''', i.e. the bijections <math>\Phi_g = \Phi (g, \cdot): X \to X</math> are [[Homeomorphism|homeomorphisms]] for every ''<math>g \in G</math>'', but the converse is not necessarily true. However, if <math>G</math> is [[Discrete group|discrete]], these two concepts coincide.

Given a ''<math>G</math>''-space, the quotient map <math>X \to X/G</math> is an [[Open and closed maps|open map]] (with respect to the [[Quotient space (topology)|quotient topology]] on <math>X/G</math>).

== Constructions ==
If <math>f: H \to G</math> is a continuous [[group homomorphism]] of topological groups, and if ''<math>X</math>'' is a ''<math>G</math>''-space, then ''<math>H</math>'' acts on ''<math>X</math>'' ''by restriction'': <math>h \cdot x = f(h) x</math>, making ''<math>X</math>'' a ''<math>H</math>''-space. Often ''<math>f</math>'' is either an inclusion or a quotient map. In particular, any topological space may be thought of as a ''<math>G</math>''-space via <math>G \to 1</math> (and ''<math>G</math>'' would act trivially).

Two basic operations are that of taking the space of points fixed by a subgroup ''<math>H</math>'' and that of forming a quotient by ''<math>H</math>''. We write <math>X^H</math> for the set of all ''<math>x</math>'' in ''<math>X</math>'' such that <math>hx = x</math>. For example, if we write <math>F(X, Y)</math> for the set of continuous maps from a ''<math>G</math>''-space ''<math>X</math>'' to another ''<math>G</math>''-space ''<math>Y</math>'', then, with the action <math>(g \cdot f)(x) = g f(g^{-1} x)</math>,
<math>F(X, Y)^G</math> consists of ''<math>f</math>'' such that <math>f(g x) = g f(x)</math>; i.e., ''<math>f</math>'' is an [[equivariant map]]. We write <math>F_G(X, Y) = F(X, Y)^G</math>. Note, for example, for a ''<math>G</math>''-space ''<math>X</math>'' and a closed subgroup ''<math>H</math>'',  <math>F_G(G/H, X) = X^H</math>.
